en: Preface to the Thirteen Chapters on Forging Discourse Why do I forge discourse on Chan and model it after the *Sunzi*? To govern a state with the orthodox and to employ troops with the extraordinary—this is the certainty of the words from beneath the pillar [the *Daodejing*].
Within the Buddha-dharma, those who occupy positions of authority govern the monastic community as they would a state, employing skillful means (*upāya*) as their stratagems.

To train the assembly of Chan practitioners is like employing an army: the alternating use of the "unusual" (qi) and the "standard" (zheng) is the unchanging Way. That single act of holding up the flower was the progenitor of military strategy.
Though the Seven Patriarchs of the Western Heaven and the Two or Three Founders of this Land revealed profound principles, they were in secret accord with the teachings of Sun Tzu and Wu Qi.
It reached the point where the "horse colt" (Maca) trampled [the enemy], like the military campaigns of Li Guangbi, wherein the defensive fortifications were transformed in an instant.

Subsequently, the various elders—Huangbo, Linji, Muzhou, Yunmen, Fenyang, Ciming, Dongshan, Yuanwu, and others—employed the strategic maneuvers of war exclusively, alternating between the void and the real, and between killing and giving life.
Reaching the time of Miaoxi, he took sole command of the bamboo staff and deployed extraordinary tactics on a grand scale; his disciples were most numerous, and thus the Five Houses were established.
Each established its own fundamental principles; their tactics were refined and rigorous, firm and indestructible, such that the art of war was complete.
From the Yuan dynasty through the mid-Ming period, these methods of training had fallen into ruin; people were treated like cold ashes or withered wood, being slaughtered in mass pits.
Fortunately, the Elder Tiantong Wu took up the three-foot sword of the Dharma to open up the territories of the Chan school, and the Elder Sanfeng Zang followed him, restoring them.

Re-establishing the fundamental principles, he once again brandished the bamboo cane to forge and refine his disciples. These dragon-elephants among men emerged from the fray like those who charge through enemy lines.

My late master at Lingyin further added versatility and adaptability; employing various methods of "cracking and pecking," they deployed a myriad of strategies and diverse approaches, with extraordinary tactics emerging in profusion.

The military treatises are thus rendered even more comprehensive. In the past, while I resided at Banshou, I gained considerable insight into their methods. Later, I settled in seclusion on Mount Kuang, dwelling near Mount Ou.
With empty fists and bare hands, and without a single soldier or rank to rely upon, I did not hesitate to devise my own system.

I innovated the techniques of moving with the crowd, striking, shifting, seizing, pecking, hacking, and cleaving. These were immediately and greatly effective, despite the hardships encountered on the field.
The battle was fought and victory was proclaimed with many captives; the methods employed were truly extreme in their eccentricity and cruelty.
Reflecting on this, I considered that regardless of whether a person's faculties are sharp or dull, if they encounter the method of forging [the mind], all can attain awakening.

Yet, because most people cling to fixed methods and do not extend a hand at the edge of the precipice, even those with talent often lament being left behind. Thus, I did not dare to keep it secret, but have composed this as "Forging Zen" (Duan Chan).
I have spoken thus to propagate the School of the Patriarchs. Although the masters and veteran monks of old may have obtained this teaching, they were not necessarily able to put it into practice.
Far from practicing it, some even derided and criticized it. Those who first sat upon the curved throne possessed bodies of heroic strength and spirits of fierce acuity;
by relying on these military insignia and training with diligent effort, they will surely awaken many people and produce great Dharma generals—this is my aspiration.
With the dark halberd and armor, one forever manifests martial strength; with the banners of the five ranks, there shall be no laying down of arms.
Whether they know me or condemn me, I do not begrudge it; thus, one might well call me the Chan School’s Sun Tzu.
Recorded on the first day of the first month of the year of Xinchou by the monk Yuanyun Jixian of Yunju, residing at Huishan,

A Solemn Account of the Thirteenth Dhyāna-Gate:
Forging through Refinement,
authored by Huisan Jiezhao of Zhenru Chan Monastery on Mount Yunju in Nan-kang, Jiangxi.
A man of firm vows who endures suffering is the foremost among elders.
According to the true station of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he ought to succeed to the ancestral legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
according to his role as a teacher and model for humans and devas, he ought to open the eyes of humans and devas. What are the eyes of humans and devas? It is the Buddha.
The nature [of Buddhahood] has already been established. What, then, is the practice of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? It is the attainment of this personhood;

yet, if one is an elder and yet cannot cause sentient beings to awaken to their Buddha-nature, this is called "stealing the name. If one occupies the correct position and yet cannot broaden the talent of those who become Buddhas and Patriarchs, this is called "usurping the position.
However, if one wishes to cause sentient beings to awaken to their Buddha-nature, then that mind must necessarily...
It is suffering. If one does not scrutinize and strip away [delusions] to the utmost, exhausting every skillful means (*upāya*), the Buddha-nature of sentient beings cannot be realized.
If one wishes to expand the pool of talent for the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one’s own person must necessarily labor;

if one does not apply diligent vigor and exert oneself with the intensity of applying needles and awls, the talent for the Dharma-gate cannot be obtained. Therefore, those who act as elders must first give rise to the Great Resolve.
One must first establish great vows and then manifest the great capacity and exert the great function. What are these vows?
Initially, as an elder, one should direct them toward the dragons and devas and appeal to the Buddhas and Patriarchs:

"If I can cause sentient beings to awaken to their Buddha-nature, then even if it requires grinding my bones and sinews and exhausting my spirit—like carving a path through a mountain—I shall exert all my strength and devote myself to this task; I must not [desist]."

This is the proper course. If one can broaden the gateway of the Dharma and cultivate talent, then even if one must practice [the discipline] morning and evening, forgetting sleep and food, or endure hardships like biting snow and swallowing felt, one should not shrink from it.

Consider those in the human world who, as parents, desire virtuous descendants: they first cultivate their own virtue and accumulate goodness, extensively practicing hidden acts of merit, before obtaining a child.
Thus, they swaddled him, nurtured him, and cared for him; as he grew older, they engaged tutors for him to oversee his studies.
Only after many decades of diligent toil did he finally become accomplished—how bitter was their heart!
When they thought of a martial officer wishing to achieve fame and merit on the frontiers, he would surely forget his head and heels, cast himself into ditches and ravines, and endure frost and dew.
They encounter thorns and brambles; they don heavy armor and wield sharp weapons; they sleep with their spears as pillows and their breastplates as bolsters; they penetrate deep into barren lands.

Having undergone a hundred battles, their fingers fall off and their skin cracks, and their bellies are covered with arrowheads. Only after experiencing ten thousand deaths for the sake of a single life do they finally achieve fame and glory in a single day.
Their toil for the sake of the body is indeed great. Being so weary and suffering, it is only right that everyone, upon hearing of this wind, should avoid it and look toward the cliffs [to retreat].

And yet they withdraw. Among all people of antiquity and today, those who ultimately find bitter tea and dock leaves palatable and show no concern, or who tread upon boiling water and fire without protest, do so because that which they plot is great, that upon which they rely is weighty, and the achievement of their merit is immense. How much more so for those who act as elders:
their Way lies in serving as a bridge across the three realms of existence and rescuing the four classes of beings, thereby augmenting the life of wisdom for the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past.
To open the eyes of the beings of this great earth—what a weighty responsibility! Yet you look upon such toil with regret and cherish it as a burden.

To produce those who teach and establish martial merit is already lowly; having already come to cherish such toil, you must surely dwell in seclusion with hands folded in idleness, cutting yourself off from the stream of Chan.

You nourish your dignity and dwell in luxury, finding self-satisfaction in ease and tranquility, treating the monastic groves as mere guesthouses and regarding the assembly of Chan practitioners with indifference.
It would be like the customs of the Hu and Yue peoples regarding winter and summer garments—merely following the literal text.

How could this not be a grave offense against the Buddhas and Patriarchs, a source of shame before the Dragons and Devas, and a betrayal of one’s own teachers? One would truly be a sinner against the Dharma-gate. As it is said in the teachings:

"A Bodhisattva, for the sake of a single sentient being, undergoes great toil and suffering throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, never feeling weary or disheartened. Yet nowadays, among the Zen community, there may be only dozens, or perhaps...
Whether it be a hundred or a thousand, when the machinery [of practice] stands before them, how could it concern only a single person? It is further said:

"For the sake of sentient beings, Bodhisattvas relinquish their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains, as well as their flesh, blood, hands, and feet, filling the entire earth and piling up like Mount Sumeru;

yet they do not, on account of such suffering, retreat or lose their Great Resolve. How much more so for those who refine themselves in meditation—exerting their sinews and toiling their bones, drinking ice-cold water [in austerity].
To compare those who consume bitter herbs with those who sacrifice their heads, eyes, blood, and flesh:

even if the latter numbered in the tens, hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions, how could they ever equal a ten-thousandth part of a bodhisattva? Once one has entered this gate, who would not regard themselves as a man of knowledge (*jñānin*)?

Once one has become an elder, who would not take it upon themselves to be a Buddha or a patriarch? Occupying such a position, one must perform its corresponding duties; bearing such a title, one must fulfill its requirements.
In truth, those who practice Zen are the essential requisites for the Elder to achieve Buddhahood. Forging [the mind] is truly the great key by which the Patriarchs have gained people.
Without diligent forging, one will certainly be unable to open the eyes of sentient beings and gain them.
Without giving rise to a vow, one will certainly be unwilling to endure suffering for the sake of forging. Therefore:
Before setting forth the methods of cultivation, one must first firmly resolve to make vows. Once the vows are established, the fundamental basis is rectified;
therefore, it is said that firm vows are primary.
Discerning the Vessel and Bestowing Instruction, Part Two:

If one wishes to forge those in the assembly through meditation, one must first demonstrate true inquiry. Before applying the tongs and hammer, one must first discern the capacity of the vessel. Linji said:
"In this tradition of mine, I sever the three types of root-capacities. I may seize the environment, or seize the person, or seize the dharma, or seize them all together."
"Or both may not seize [the student]. This is the essential method for testing the capacity of the practitioner (*kī*). During the Tang dynasty, the Chan style was at its zenith;
practitioners were extraordinary, and when the ancient masters received people, they employed the total function of their entire capacity to suddenly sever the life-root (*mūla*).

They used exclusively living mechanisms (*jīvita-kī*) and entirely lacked dead methods (*mṛta-dharma*). From the Song dynasty onward, the use of *hwadu* (critical phrases) in Zen meditation arose, and dead methods were established. Nevertheless...

In these final dharma ages, human faculties have become increasingly inferior, while intellectual cleverness has grown deeper; madness and disorder have become more chaotic, and meditative concentration and wisdom have become shallower.
Those who preside over the Dharma, wishing to cause the assembly of Chan practitioners to expand their innate nature and penetrate the firm barrier, cannot help but employ "dead methods.
Such is the exigency of the times. However, if they do not know how to employ them skillfully, then even "living methods" will all become dead methods. If one can employ them skillfully...
When employed, within the midst of the method of death there is naturally the method of life. What is this method of life? It is the discernment of the capacities of those present.
When the assembly of Chan practitioners enters the gate, one first uses the "eye" to weigh their faculties and determine the relative caliber of their talent;
next, one uses the "probing pole and shadow-grass" to test the depth of their study. Establishing host and guest, with one question and one answer, they draw out the thread as it comes, observing—
By knowing whether [the student] possesses [the capacity] or not, one perceives their spiritual faculties (*indriya*).

If someone of the highest caliber (*agratama-yānika*) arrives, the master immediately employs the claws and fangs of a lion, the majestic ferocity of an elephant king, tossing a golden ring and hurling a *kṣiptaka* thorn to observe whether they can penetrate the barrier;

thus, the handle remains with the master. Once the faculties are ascertained, only then does he order them to enter the hall. Having entered the meditation hall, they should immediately proceed to practice.

In the meditation hall, he provides *huatou* (critical phrases) according to the capacities of practitioners—whether superior, middling, or inferior. For those who have already traveled through various regions and possess established *huatou*, he may refine them, shift them, or correct them.
Although there is not a single fixed method in his approach, the *huatou* remains precise and the compass point of the mind is set.
Some say that there are cases where *huatou* is not employed at all, proceeding instead directly with the "immediate" [action] of Deshan or Linji.
Regarding the one who meets people with a staff and a shout: it is said, "It is indeed marvelous; however, it views the capacities of others as too high and cannot be applied universally.
As for the one who, regardless of whether a person's faculties are sharp or dull or how many practitioners there are, employs only a single *huatou* without changing it:
it is said, "It is indeed uniform; however, it views the capacities of others as too mixed. Even if one practices...
Yet many do not obtain benefit. Let me explain the reason for this. Not employing the *huatou* (critical phrase) is indeed direct and incisive, free from any lingering attachments;

however, while this was acceptable for people of the past, it is not permissible in the present age. Why is this? Because the faculties and capacities of those ancients were lofty and superior, and their power of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) was strong;
once they encountered a renowned master or great craftsman who provided guidance through the striking of staffs or shouts, [they immediately attained realization]. One...
Faith is eternal faith; there is no further ambiguity. A single penetration is eternal penetration; there is no further reversal. This is why it is functional.
Nowadays, people employ their most profound intellectual cleverness and their most chaotic turbulence, yet they do not use the *huatou* (critical phrase) as a heavy seal and a tight lock.

With piercing admonitions and deep probes, they cause one’s emotions to wither and wisdom to be exhausted. Only when one suddenly turns over can one employ the single stroke of "flashing lightning upon striking flint" as the gateway to the teaching.
Even if one should manage to take this up, it mostly belongs to the realm of mere shadows and reflections;

for regarding the pivot of words and phrases—the very lifeblood of the patriarchs—one has not yet seen through them at all. To claim such a state as "awakening" will lead to repeated reversals in the future.
It can be said that [such methods] are therefore not to be employed. This does not mean they are entirely unusable; rather, they must not be applied indiscriminately. Huanglong told Huitang:
"If you do not contemplate the *huatou* (critical phrase) but instead employ a hundred stratagems to search for it, seeking to have yourself see and approve of it, then I am burying you.
Is this not to be believed? To employ only a single *huatou* seems equal, simple, and direct, yet...

This has already been distinguished. Nevertheless, among the assembly of Chan practitioners, there are those of keen and dull faculties; their dispositions may be pure or impure; their faith in the Way may be shallow or deep;
and their duration of study may be long or short. One who buys a hat must fit it to the head; one who drives a wedge must look at the hole.

This is the natural course of things. For those who should practice counting the breaths (*ānāpāna*), one instructs them to contemplate white bones; for those who should contemplate the bones, one instructs them to count the breaths.
Even during the Buddha’s own lifetime, it was not possible to realize the fruits of the path; how much more so in the Age of Dharma Decline (*mofa*)?

One who clarifies the Great Dharma examines the "climate" to apply the tongs and hammer, and recognizes the shifts and transformations to employ the chisel and drill; thus, all three faculties become sharp. This enables one to act without being hindered by their dullness.

Whether dull or pure, mixed or coarse, shallow or deep, long-standing or brief, they merely employ a single *huatou* to bind the student—drawing lines on the ground to create a prison, or nailing down a stake while rowing a boat.
Those who are high are suppressed and cannot descend; those who are low stand on tiptoe and cannot reach it.
This is what is meant by a "living method" becoming a "dead method. Miaoxi said: "The Great Dharma of a true spiritual friend..."
"Clearly! To point out to others only the place of one's own self-realization will surely blind their eyes—is this not what is meant?
If so, when instructing on the *huatou*, what method should be employed? It is likewise said that one must simply sever the three types of faculties.
For a beginner practitioner, the *huatou* is extremely profound and difficult; they will inevitably encounter resistance, and you must cause them to have at least some degree of 'gnawing' [upon it]."
Chew upon it to bring forth its root. Those whose spirit and bearing are brilliant and heroic may find the "head-word" too relaxed, which easily fosters conceptual speculation;
you must cause it to stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high to sever all攀缘 (pān-yuán, clinging/seeking). It is like "all phenomena returning to the One," or "before one's parents were born."
From "dying" and "burning," down to every single instance and object before one's eyes, these may be employed by both the wise and the foolish, yet they are most convenient for beginners.

Nanquan’s "Three Are Not," Dahui’s "Bamboo Ruler," and the statement that whether one speaks or does not speak, one receives thirty blows—whether one acts thus or does not act thus, all are incorrect—and so forth:
although these may be used by those of high or low capacity, they are [most suited to] the heroic...

This is for the sake of spiritual efficacy. Furthermore, when there are those who hold their heads high and wear horns, whose insight and realization are fierce and strong, the master’s claws and fangs must be all the more virulent.
Sometimes he uses skillful means, joy, or anger to sever their life-root; sometimes he employs convoluted and paradoxical speech to strip away their secret hoardings.
What Linji called "the whole body" or "half the body," and the metaphors of the lion and the elephant king, were all intended for such as these.
This depends entirely on how the master employs his function; it cannot be transmitted through words.

In short, although there are many different types of *huatou*, each must have a subtle "lock" at its upper end. Once there is this lock, when the student applies their mind, the four gates are blocked and the six paths are utterly severed.
At the lower end, during the stage of interrogation, the arousal of the state of doubt (*yiqing*) will necessarily occur.

"True. Once the state of doubt is genuine, the capacity for awakening will surely penetrate through to the bottom. Dongshan established the analogy of a father setting a lock on a chest while his son breaks through the siege;

is this not a secret not [easily] transmitted? Nevertheless, there are also those whose capacities and conditions are suited to the kōan responses, such as "Three pounds of flax," "A dried piece of excrement," "The monk’s robe from Qingzhou," "The cypress tree in the courtyard," and even "The dog."

Some individuals lack the Buddha-nature; yet there are also those whose capacities are such that they are suited for the application of the teaching's "trigger" (ji). For instance, when one enters the gate, [the master] immediately strikes with a staff;

when one advances through the gate, he immediately shouts. Mazu’s reception of Yunmen and Fenyang’s reception of Ciming are examples of this, where, time and again, the gateway to great enlightenment was opened.
This also depends on how the master conducts his household affairs; there is no fixed method for death [or liberation]. Occasionally, there are masters who do not understand the essential pivot;
they merely instruct people to investigate such questions as: "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? "What is one's original face? or "What is the student’s own self?
This leaves the upper part unsecured, like calling out into the empty air; when the master strikes the blow, [the student is lost].
It is not urgent. Those from families of learning harbor doubts and lack power; they drift in stagnant waters, failing to awaken even in their white-haired old age.

Their sitting in sickness lies precisely here—how can one not lament this? That which most misleads people is when those who have newly entered the gate of Chan, having not yet fundamentally awakened, are immediately made to investigate such stories as Nanquan’s killing of the cat, Baizhang’s wild fox, Danxia’s burning of the Buddha, and the woman emerging from samādhi. This is truly...
To force square wood through a round hole is to waste human time; it is worlds apart from the truth. Is it not fitting, then, to call this "fabrication"?

Therefore, for those who wish to refine the assembly of practitioners, it is of the utmost importance as the primary requirement for entering the gate to carefully discern their capacities and select the appropriate *huatou*, so that both the high and low may find what suits them and both the sharp and dull may be equally aided.

Regarding the third point, "Entering the Room for Search and Seizure," once the *huatou* has been shown, one must immediately instruct the practitioner to investigate it. There are two methods of investigation: the first is called "peaceful and harmonious" (*heping*), and the second is called "fierce and intense" (*mengli*).
As for those who investigate in a peaceful and harmonious manner, it is difficult for them to achieve awakening; yet even if they do gain some understanding, they fail to transcend the ordinary.
It will inevitably be weak. For those who practice with fierce intensity, it is easy for realization to be awakened;

once they enter the furnace and forge, the person who emerges will surely be strong. What is the reason for this? It is because if one employs tranquility (*śamatha*) alone, the process becomes gentle and lax;
it can only suppress superficial emotions and purge coarse cognitions. After a long time of maturation, it merely comes to rest in a state of pure clarity and total purity.
To strike at the gate and beat upon the joints [of the teaching] will surely be without hope. Therefore it is said: "The arising of realization is difficult.
As for the phrase "a bean exploding from cold ashes," even if one were perfectly complete without any leakage, they would still be a dead man on level ground;

upon encountering the harsh hands and feet of the thorny courtyard, they would immediately melt away like ice or crumble like tiles. How much less could such a person endure great matters, shoulder the great burden, and lead the assembly without collapsing?

How perilous! Therefore it is said that "the person emerges weak. If you wish to seek one who can sever [the matter] with a snap, break it with a crack, turn back from within a fierce flame, or cut off their life amidst a steep precipice—one who can withstand being thrown down, struck, and battered while remaining calm and unmoved—then nothing but a fierce and sharp inquiry will suffice.
Although such fierceness is superior, there is fear that its strength may not endure long; if you hope to achieve results within a set number of days, [you must apply yourself with such intensity].
Success can only be achieved by establishing a fixed period for the seven-day intensive practice (*qijie*).

When the seven-day retreat is established with a time limit, not only do those who are physically robust and heroic exert themselves a hundredfold, but even the timid and the weak will surely die of resolve upon seeking entry into the protective community;

they will even be willing to sacrifice their bodies and give up their lives. Therefore, the seven-day retreat must not be undertaken without a limit. If one wishes to initiate the seven-day retreat, one must enter the room (*rushì*).

This must come first. Entering the room is not merely a matter of formalities; since the Elder has taken the task of forging [the practitioners] as his business, he should maintain a rigorous mind, apply himself with deep intent, establish rules strictly, and exert effort with meticulous care.

Before desiring to enter the hall, one must first know the names and appearances of the meditation assembly members, as well as their respective original *hua-tou* (critical phrases for inquiry), and only then may one bestow [instruction].
This is merely physical exercise. Failing to recognize the person, even if one gathers for ninety days, the relationship remains like that of strangers on a road;
what is called "entering retreat" (jie-zhi) is then nothing more than a bustling of the monastery gates, which benefits the Chan assembly in no way.

Even if one recognizes the person, yet is not familiar with their fundamental inquiry (ben-can), then when the Elder descends to the hall intending to apply pressure and scrutiny, there will be no way to reach them, as the handle [of their practice] has already...

It is not within one's hands; thus, the general conventions of the Chan school emerged. What are these general conventions? Regarding the Chan regulations for winter and summer retreats, all matters are entrusted to the administrative officers (*zhishi*).
These officers strictly uphold the rules of the incense board: if a monk sits, they allow him to succumb to drowsiness or distraction; if he walks, they permit him to become weary at his own pace.
Even a senior elder (*changlao*) who possesses dignity shall not fail to enter the hall unless invited by the administrative officer with the sounding of the *qing* gong. That is to say—
As for those who break the rule for the sake of the assembly: sometimes they enter the hall once every day or two days; sometimes once every three or five days.
The indolent may go ten days or half a month, and there are even those who do not enter the hall until the end of their term.

When the Elder enters the hall, the attendants stand in solemn rows like the formal procession at a government office; the drawing of lots and the calling of names are like the procedures of an official court.

When the officials mark the attendance rolls, the senior elder (Changlao) does not recognize the names or appearances of the Zen practitioners, nor does he know their fundamental *huatou* (critical phrase).
Unable to avoid his responsibility, he must pose a question or present a *gong'an* (public case) as a stopgap measure; this is the most egregious of clichés.
Those who have long experienced the Zen assembly possess slippery wit and a practiced path, managing matters as they arise even before the elder has spoken.
Upon entering the hall, his mind was already colored by red and yellow (with preconceptions), and his mental draft was already complete.

Furthermore, the Elder did not employ the maneuvers of "seizing, releasing, killing, or giving life" characteristic of the essential principles of the school to search for the meaning of his phrases or expose his hidden traps.

He merely sought a slick, ready-made response, regarding mere verbal dexterity as spiritual brilliance. As soon as a question was posed, he would manage to mumble one or two forced words and pass the time until the next session.
For those who have already practiced for a long time, this may seem beneficial but is actually of no benefit at all. As for the ignorant beginners, they have never even set eyes upon Zen texts;
their dullness and distraction have not yet been eliminated, and they have not yet mastered the contemplation of the *huatou*.

When the Elder descends from the hall, nineteen out of twenty such people will stand far back, hiding themselves, not daring to approach. Even if they were to be pointed out, he would not interrogate them.
To investigate a *kōan* while fundamentally lacking true inquiry is like asking a wood-carrying laborer about the affairs of the Hall of Central Secretaries;
with head fixed and eyes straight, one merely endures one or two blows before escaping with one's life. This is the most useless of all things useless for a beginner.
Once the elder has finished his formal inspection, he returns to his quarters, while the assembly of monks, in turn, turns back toward their own delusive thoughts.
They sit inside [the trap], drowned in stagnant water; otherwise, they merely pass their days distracted by dullness and agitation.
Among those who seek to find the path through diligent practice, not even one or two in a hundred succeed, let alone achieve thorough awakening. This is what is called a "commonplace routine."
These good spiritual friends use such clichés to deal with people; while it may be easy for them, how can the karmic consciousness of the Chan assembly be cleared away over vast kalpas?
How can their false views be eradicated? How can the mass of doubt be shattered?
And how can they escape birth and death? All of this is the fault of not recognizing the person and not knowing the fundamental inquiry. If you wish to know...

The method for this lies in entering the chamber and conducting a thorough investigation. For the capacities of individuals are not uniform, and there are many varieties of distinctions among those who study under a teacher.
Though one may have received a *huatou*, some lack the resolve to investigate it; some fail to attain realization because they have not applied their whole heart;

some possess the resolve yet fail to give rise to the "doubt-mass" (*yiqing*); some find themselves entangled in delusive thoughts as soon as the *huatou* is raised; and others may have investigated for many years.
Yet they do not understand what the practice of *gongfu* (spiritual effort) truly is. Some employ the logical paths of the sutras and treatises to match them with the *huatou* (critical phrase);
some merely borrow the *huatou* to dispel deluded thoughts; some hide their roots within the "armour of non-action"; some stubbornly assume mastery as their sovereign;
and some mistake silent, seamless stillness for ultimate realization. All of this stems from a lack of [true] people [to guide them].

Rectify and correct this. If there is no genuine doubt within, it will lead to many ailments. Therefore, at every moment of entering the room, you must investigate each point one by one and sweep away each obstacle one by one.
Untie their adhesions and remove their fetters; cast out obstructions and polish away dullness. Cut through the threads that bind them to their companions and attachments;
treat their chronic, fatal maladies. Direct them toward true inquiry, and the path will surely be set right.

If one does not strip away [all conceptualizations] until they are utterly exhausted, but instead hands over a "head-word" in a muddled manner or grants a public case (kōan) in a superficial way, and if the student is unskilled at applying the mind, then they will desire the orthodox while leaning toward the heterodox, desire purity while leaning toward defilement, and desire clarity while leaning toward darkness;

their entire being will be afflicted by the diseases of Zen that cannot be cured. For this reason, when entering the inner chamber for instruction, it is vital that the Elder leaves [the matter] in secret.
Once the mind can recognize the person’s name and appearance, and record the person’s original inquiry,
one may then gradually apply the methods of forging and refining to remove their karmic hindrances of meditation (*zenbyō*) and lead them onto the correct path.
The fourth lecture on guidance in the hall:
you have already entered the room and investigated with precision; there are no longer any mistaken paths. However, for one who studies the Way, it is like rowing a boat against the current:

Rolling and turning; vivid and alert. One must ensure that the student has no place to set foot, for then it will not be difficult to sever their life-root.

It is like an arrow about to leave the string—it requires but a single nudge; or like a spring about to gush from a conduit—it remains only at the threshold.

A single phrase. An elder did not hinder him, allowing him to ask again; perhaps by substituting a single word he attained immediate awakening, or by changing a single character his mind became vast and clear.

Chapter Eight: Breaking Through the Barrier and Opening the Eye.

It is difficult enough to change one's fundamental nature; yet, to break through the heavy barrier and open the eyes of others requires more than the keen vision of a hawk or a dragon—it demands the skillful maneuvers of one who wields a great banner. Guide and spur them forward. If you do not provide guidance, the path will branch into diversions; if you do not spur them on, the fire will not blaze forth;
