Miaoxi said, "The diamond circle and the chestnut thorn are truly difficult to swallow and difficult to penetrate. When one reaches this point and can directly accept them, even if the Great Dharma is not yet clear, one cannot do anything about it.
He further said, "Regarding the various causes and conditions of the ancients, once the Great Dharma is clearly understood, [they are all] brought forth."

As soon as it arises, one understands it. I have often observed that people today, lacking any formal lineage of transmission, do nothing but spit upon and revile others whenever they hear them speak of the Great Dharma or the Small Dharma.
Why does Miaoxi (Wumen) labor with thousands of words and myriad phrases to exhort us toward the Great Dharma?

Is it that Miaoxi is merely fabricating these teachings, or is it that people today fail to see for themselves and thus recklessly offer their criticisms? Therefore, this is the very foundation for those who study the Way.
This has already been clarified. One should rely upon a teacher and master to study and investigate with warmth and intimacy, striving to penetrate the inner sanctum of the ancients.

When the teacher perceives that the student has thoroughly mastered the fundamental source, they must further employ subtle and secret tongs and hammers, applying deep probes and piercing stabs, ensuring that the student penetrates the steel-like eyes of the school.
Only then will there be no mutual transmission of empty echoes, and the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye will endure forever.
It has been transmitted afar through the ages. Regarding the tenth [section], the path beyond the ten directions where the practice is refined and strict:
it is not transmitted by the thousand sages. It is like a great mass of fire; who would dare to look upon it with a direct eye? It is like a coating of...
A poisonous drum—whom could one listen to with bated breath? A flash of lightning before the pivot of action already belongs to the realm of hesitation;
to claim mastery beneath a single phrase remains but a deluded view. What kind of matter is this, that you so insistently inquire after my conduct and loftily debate my merits?
However, the First Patriarch said, "One whose practice and understanding correspond is called a Patriarch.

Yunju Dengzhu said, "Having realized that which lies beyond, one then practices within this world. Yongquan said, "Those with insight are many; those who possess both practice and understanding are not one in ten thousand.
Thus, we know that the successive Patriarchs of old never regarded practice and understanding as two separate things. This is truly because...

Practice without understanding means that although one’s conduct may be refined and pure, it does not transcend the stages of gradual cultivation; even if there is spiritual cultivation, it is all termed "foolish merit.
Understanding without practice means that although one’s realization may be transcendent, it is still like carrying a single plank;
though there is an entrance to awakening, it all belongs to "mad wisdom. One has eyes but no feet; the other has a tail but no head. Neither is ultimate. This is because...

Venerable Elder, your efforts lie in forging human talent, discerning between the partial and the complete, and weighing the beginning and the end. You desire that students achieve success from start to finish;
what is the path to this? To those whose family lineage and Dharma-eye have not yet opened, you first command them to engage in investigation to forge their understanding.

You strike to the bone and beat to the marrow, applying needles and awls with merciless severity, yet your conduct remains consistently relaxed and your questioning slow and steady—this is what is meant by "merely... [the rest of the passage].
Your eyesight is correct, noble sir; I shall not speak of your conduct. Once the Great Matter is clarified, you must immediately take up practice to forge your actions.
On the Bird Path and the Mysterious Way, there is no self-interest beneath one's feet, and only through such understanding does one arrive at reality. As it is said:
"A fathom of speaking is not worth a foot of practicing. However, those who preside over the Dharma do not employ the steel-like eye of the ancestral school for trivialities.

Those who examine people merely grasp at partial knowledge and half-understood interpretations. When selecting talented individuals, there are two divergent paths within the common understanding of Chan.

Those who take the "host" (the primary subject) to be Chan simply recognize the sovereign of the body-field—the one who moves, turns, acts, and functions—as the great capacity and great function of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
They claim that whether in accord or in opposition, everything is [Chan], asserting that "activity itself is nature."

Due to this recklessness, latent tendencies (vāsanā) secretly erupt, leading eventually to a state where one makes no distinction between what is fit for consumption and what is not, nor does one discriminate between the pure and the defiled, regarding this as the Great Way.
When someone attempts to correct them, they say: "Fool! How could there be two Buddha-natures?

This is what is meant by becoming a practitioner of demonic karma through the gate of "sticky glue" (citraka). Those who take "vast emptiness" (prapañca-śūnyatā) to be Chan merely recognize the original...
Coming from nowhere, there is no substance; in a state of silent oblivion and vast emptiness, they take this as their own way of establishing a secure dwelling and sustaining their lives.
They claim there is no Buddha and no Patriarchs, that all things are empty, and call this the "ultimate point.

From this superficiality, false views find their opportunity, leading them to act with total license and without restraint, neither avoiding censure nor regarding sin and merit. When someone rebukes or admonishes them, they say:
"Shaking it off. Yet this very thing still remains. This is what is called "extinguishing cause and effect through the Zen of the iron shovel.
These two [approaches], though the errors of students, are also the fault of the teachers.

Because they do not use the fundamental principles (*gangzong*) to forge people, but instead merely seize upon shadows and glimmers to transmit them to one another, those of inferior capacity consequently give rise to heterodoxy.
This explains the dharma-gate of calamity. For if the lineage of masters is correct, the conduct and understanding of the students will necessarily be upright;

as they are transmitted from generation to generation like one vessel passing its contents to another, the source is deep and the stream is long. If the lineage of masters is not correct, the conduct and understanding of the students will necessarily be deviant;
as they are inherited and become a prevailing custom, it is like the characters "crow" (*wu*) and "who" (*an*) being mistaken for "horse" (*ma*), where a thin layer of sediment flows into a torrent.
How humble! What is meant by "inheriting the orthodox lineage"? It is when one’s insight into the Way is thoroughly penetrating and one’s conduct is likewise weighty.

Although he is an elder, in all matters he is identical to the common assembly. He purifies his person and disciplines his will; rising early and retiring late, he takes the diligent toil of former masters as his standard and guide.
Like ice and frost, like gold and jade, his practice of the Way is filled within; thus the monastic community has a model to emulate.

This is what is called "correctness. What is meant by "the lineage of the teacher being incorrect"? It refers to one whose insight into the Way is shallow and reckless, yet whose mind holds their own conduct in low esteem.
Once occupying the position of a teacher, they act in every matter differently from the rest of the assembly:

they refine their food, wear silken garments, retire early and rise late, regarding such idle ease as a refined liberation, while remaining stubborn and perverse, scolding those who practice cultivation. The entire community...
To have nothing to grasp is called "improper. Thus, from antiquity to the present, when the Buddha-dharma flourished, those of the foremost rank in practice were the elders;
yet when the True Dharma grew thin, those of the foremost rank in negligence were also the elders.
When elders revere their conduct, the dragon deities grant protection and the fourfold assembly offer sincere devotion, and thus the Buddha-dharma...
It will surely flourish. If elders abandon virtuous conduct, they will clearly incur public reproach and secretly invite divine retribution; thus, the Buddha-dharma will inevitably decline.

Indeed, the perverse and deceitful practices harbored by these elders are not limited to a single instance, yet the most extraordinary is that their conduct does not exceed that of commoners, yet they falsely project an air of grandeur to claim it is true Buddha-dharma, even going so far as to revile the Buddhas and patriarchs and lash out at the gods and spirits.

Frivolously emulating the likes of Deshan and Linji while still dwelling on the level of ordinary beings, you presume the marks of one who has attained the fruit-stage while remaining a person of the causal stage.

You frequently burn and destroy scriptures and images, and trample upon the sages and worthies, comparing yourself to Danxia, Fozhao, and Daohao, yet lacking the penetrating celestial eye of Nanquan, Guizong, Daguai, and others; thus, you recklessly slaughter and injure [the teachings] of your own accord.

It is said that among those who tread like dragons and elephants, there were no great manifestations of sovereign power such as Kumārajīva, Baozhi, Puzhao, Jidian, Jiuxian, or Lianzi, yet they recklessly consumed wine and meat, thereby violating the monastic precepts.
Little do they realize that when ancient sages act in contravention of the norm, it is the manifestation of an ancient sage;
when Buddhas and patriarchs shatter attachments, it is the emergence of a Buddha or patriarch. Though they have attained liberation...

Precious jewels appear as rags; they change the eyes of men. They carry water and drag through mud, striking away the shackles of others. Yet, while concealing their saintliness, they manifest inferiority;
following along with worldly displays, they exhibit supernatural powers. Carrying the fruit while practicing the cause, they repeatedly manifest spiritual wonders.

How could they ever act in the same way as those deluded by ignorance and darkness, sharing in their same perversions and confusion? Now, those who shoulder the burden of the Dharma-lot lack the divine power of the ancient sages.
They merely follow in their footsteps, lacking the spiritual wonders of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, yet indulge only in greed.
Are they not of the lineage of foxes and insects, who have sunk themselves into the realm of Pāpīyān? By undermining the right faith of others and destroying the Dharma-gate, they act thus.
All of this is due to the elders' use of deception, leading their dharma-heirs to imitate them; as it spreads from one to another, the demonic weeds grow ever more rampant.
Regarding karma, the ancients said: "If the father commits murder, the son will surely commit robbery.
This is because, after one has attained awakening, if one deeply enters into the fundamental principles and earnestly cultivates one's conduct, how could such a thing possibly occur? Guishan said:

"Although a student of the Way may, through conditions, attain sudden awakening to the fundamental principle in a single thought-moment, there still remain the manifest karmic consciousnesses from beginningless time that must be purified and eliminated according to the Dharma. (Hui) [continued].
The Master said: "When I first entered the Way, I presumed it would be very easy. Upon withdrawing to reflect on myself, I found my contradictions to be extreme.

Consequently, I practiced with vigor for three years before finally attaining a state where every matter accorded with principle—even reaching the level of Zhaozhou’s forty years of undistracted mental application."
Xianglin spent forty years forging everything into a single piece; Yongquan, after forty years, still had moments of wavering.
Both were matters following their awakening. The former masters were not unaware of acting in opposition or in accordance with the flow as the realm of great beings;
yet they practiced with diligent toil until old age without weariness because those who recognize the Dharma are fearful. Thus, they forged and tempered the monks so that—
To serve as a banner for future generations and a model for the Dharma-gate, one’s rigorous practice and realization—how could these be neglected?
Regarding the tenth point on refining one's studies:
the Great Way does not reside in words, yet without words there is no way to manifest the Way. The Buddha-dharma does not reside in mere learning, yet without learning...

There is no way to clarify the Dharma. Those who truly concern themselves with birth and death cannot distance themselves from names or sever themselves from signs; they must strike at their own selves to engage in practice.

Yet, if one gallops after the study of doctrine, abandoning the root to pursue the branches, then even keen intelligence cannot overcome karma, and vast erudition will not exempt one from the wheel of suffering.
Moreover, the Way of learning is profound and vast, without end; its mysteries are deep and recondite, difficult to exhaust. Confucian scholars may reach white hair [in pursuit of it].
Even those who exhaustively study the scriptures still find them insufficient; how much more so for those who, begrudging the mere clipping of their nails, seek transcendence?

Nevertheless, if one wishes to penetrate the religious teachings, distinguish between the ancient and the modern, clarify the fundamental principles, recognize the application of spiritual capacities, serve as a guide for future generations, and make definitive judgments regarding the realms of humans and devas, then learning is indeed indispensable.
Now, learning is of two kinds: internal and external. What is internal learning? It fills the dragon palaces and overflows the oceans.
The "Treasury" (Zàng) comprises the Indian and Chinese lands; it consists of the seventeen hundred koṭis of worn-out vines—the entirety of worldly compositions.

What are the external studies? They include the *Féndiǎn* and *Qiūsuo*, the *Shīshū* and the Six Arts, the repositories of the *Zhìzhōu* and *Jīnchái*, the works of the national gates and famous mountains, the historical scholarship of the *Chūnqiū*, and the various masters and hundred schools—these constitute the worldly [treasury].
All the canonical scriptures are [the means for this]. If one does not study the internal [teachings], one will not be familiar with one's fundamental vocation;

how then can one transcend the world to benefit sentient beings? If one does not study the external [teachings], one will have no knowledge of Confucian arts; thus, one cannot respond appropriately to the affairs of the mundane world.

This causes people to say that those of the Chan school are all empty and superficial, lacking in learning, dull-witted, and ignorant. How then can they extract the heart-essence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and win over the world?
What a preeminent figure among both the clergy and the laity! Some have said: "The ultimate point transcends all names and words.

Since the World-Honored One clearly stated that 'no reliance is placed on words and letters' and that there is a 'separate transmission outside the teachings,' Caoxi said, 'The wondrous principle of the Buddhas has nothing to do with words and letters.
And Yaoshan never preached the Dharma, saying, 'The sutras have their own masters; the treatises have their own masters. Why should one find Yaoshan strange?'"
"Monk, you now wish to have others polish your studies; you must certainly strive to master names and phrases, gaining a superficial knowledge of the classics and histories.

By hunting for words, fishing for citations, wielding the lead pencil and brush, and manipulating red and yellow ink, you will transform the Chan gate into mere literary composition and increase intellectual understanding to ruin the ancestral school.
This will surely begin with you. I replied: "The two characters 'investigation' (can) and 'study' (xue) were established by the various patriarchs; they possess their own sequential order."
Although one must not emphasize study while abandoning *can* (investigation), nor may one exclusively practice *can* while neglecting study.

While the fundamental source remains unclarified and the mass of doubt remains unbroken, regardless of whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, all must undergo rigorous *kan-hua* (investigating the critical phrase).

At the very moment of such investigation, all names and words are swept away and all knowledge and views are severed; there are no gates in any direction, and iron mountains block the path. Suspended between the eyebrows—
The sword strikes and blood splatters against the Brahma-heaven; a single stroke of the character "one" (元) remains, yet poison has entered the heart and grit has settled in the eyes.
What does this have to do with mere scholarship? As for attaining enlightenment through practice: it is like smashing a crystal bottle to release a falcon from the vast heavens.
It covers heaven and earth while striking the void to produce resonance; it penetrates sound and form as a dragon roars from a withered tree. All...
The words and phrases of the Patriarchs are merely the sound of a bowl clinking; the doctrines and meanings of the Three Vehicles are nothing more than a tethering stake for a donkey.

When Deshan attained great enlightenment, he said: "Exhausting all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the vast void; exhausting all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss.
He caused [his students] to set aside names and words once and undergo a "great death," seeking that which returns after having been severed.
"Awakened! Is there such vast clarity and such extraordinary wonder? This is precisely why one must not study it superficially while abandoning inquiry.
When the mass of doubt is finally shattered and the fundamental ground is illuminated, the mind of *nirvāṇa* is easy to understand, yet the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify.
An ancient said: 'Within the mind of *nirvāṇa*, there is infinite subtlety; within the wisdom of differentiation, [therein lies the ultimate]. "

There are infinite complexities and contradictions. The karmic conditions of the patriarchs are like interlocking rings and hooks; the essential tenets of the Five Houses are like military talismans kept within one’s breast.

Their words and meanings conceal their sharpness, polished like gold and ground like jade so that nothing is revealed. Existence and non-existence are intertwined, as difficult to penetrate as spiderwebs and ant trails.
How could this be merely for those who stand exposed in the open or have grasped but a single peg? This is called "one-sided understanding."

One hundred [cases] concluded. To achieve thorough and complete penetration is indeed difficult; it relies entirely upon diligent study and accumulated reflection. This is especially true for one who aspires to the position of an elder (*sthavira*).
Once you wish to occupy this seat, you must resolve doubts and pose challenging questions to clarify matters with the fourfold assembly.

Regarding verses, stanzas, and prose sayings, as well as the critical examination, the selection of cases, and the delivery of *fayu* (dharma-talks) by other masters, you must scrutinize them with students and provide insightful commentary to open up their meaning.
This cannot be a matter of arbitrarily filling the void with excuses. Furthermore, the magnificent texts of the Tripiṭaka possess a vast and boundless ocean of meaning;
the precepts of the Five Divisions are as profound as a deep sea. These are fully contained within the jade cases and transmitted in the libraries of the Brahmā-heaven.

How can they be relegated to high shelves, while one merely lumps everything together under the name of "Chan" (Dhyāna), content to remain like one blind from birth, and in idle recklessness, treat all things with arrogance? This is contrary to the Dharma.

Regarding the gate of the scriptural canon, these matters are blurred; as for the language of worldly affairs, his entire being is pitch black. When questioned on the religious teachings (*jiaozong*), he resorts to makeshift excuses;
when consulted on the classical precedents, his face flushes red and his speech falters. When he opens his mouth, his cries sound like those of a jackal.

To touch their tongues [and speak] would reveal them as a base breed, like mute sheep. They immediately seek to don the robes and sweep the floors, squatting upon curved couches while claiming to belong to the lineages of Yang or Zheng, deceiving and intimidating the common folk by saying they belong to such-and-such a school or such-and-such a branch. Are they not truly putting people to shame? The *Book of Rites* says:
"If speech lacks refinement, its practice will not travel far. Therefore, those who forge disciples and bind them to a single, rigid method are merely practitioners of the academic schools.

Many do not exhaust their full potential. Among those who mold and forge human talent, there are those whose literary brilliance is not matched by other virtues; such individuals often fail to find their proper application within the Dharma-gate.

Setting aside those who are like blind men feeling an elephant—utterly lacking even a nostril—even those whose "nostrils" (essential faculties) are correct, yet who are as wooden and dull as they are without literary grace, may have a surplus when dwelling in seclusion, but are insufficient for benefiting sentient beings. Like a broken jar, they are no longer fit vessels; such is the category of human character.

Those who are morally corrupt need no further mention. Even among those of upright character, if their learning is meager, they may be fit for personal cultivation but cannot be entrusted with the task of upholding the Dharma.
While this is partly due to the fixed capacities of the student, it is also the fault of the teacher’s failure to provide sufficient refinement in the furnace of instruction.
The most biased among them take the fact that Master Caoxi was illiterate as a shield for themselves.

When he saw a student briefly investigating the past and present, he immediately rebuked him as one who has "abandoned his home to wander in confusion. He took Deshan’s words for "loosening adhesions" (*jie-nian*) as literal doctrine.

When he saw a fellow resident slightly studying the sutras and teachings, he immediately cursed him as one who "counts treasures and calculates grains of sand," regarding the long-term practice of sitting in death and burying oneself in a ghost cave as the true Buddha and true Dharma.
Furthermore, when he saw any of the ancestral masters of the past who had produced even slight writings, [he disparaged them].
Such individuals are immediately disparaged as followers of the "school of intellectual understanding" (*zhijie zongtu*).

Consequently, Tian Tong, Xuedou, Yongming, Foyin, Mingjiao, Juefan, Miaoxi, Zhongfeng, Liaoran, San-sheng, Quan, and Wanjuan were all disparaged as mere "scholarly spiritual friends" (*wenzi shanzhishi*).
Is this not a grievous injustice? Now, did Ashvaghosa and Nagarjuna ever fail to compose treatises? Yet they transmitted [the Dharma] directly and exclusively.
As for the Sixth Patriarch, although Caoxi claimed not to know how to read or write, his preaching was like clouds pouring forth;

his golden chapters and jade-like verses have served as a standard for ten thousand generations. Yet you use this as a pretext to hide your own lack of roots, leading beginners and later generations into absurdity and the abandonment of study.
It is truly lamentable that there are even those who cannot recognize a single character. Alas!

Within the vast literary currents and ocean of learning in this world of heaven and earth, though men of extraordinary talent and unique ability may be said to possess a rare vital energy (*keng-ki*), those whose very bones are those of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and whose chests are filled with brocade and embroidery, are never lacking within the Dharma-gate.
Even among those of inferior capacity, if they are skilled in composition and refinement, they too may [attain excellence].
To achieve thorough penetration, one must value spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). One should refine oneself according to their guidance:
first forging the gateway to awakening, and subsequently honing one's academic studies, so that one possesses both substance and expression, as well as virtue and learning.

When such a person emerges to propagate the teachings and act as a stabilizing pillar against the decaying current, the Dharma-gate will not be reduced to ruin, and the "Old Barbarian" (the Buddha) may truly have cause for hope.
Section Twelve: Refining Talent. Mingjiao Sōng said:
"There is nothing more honored than the Way (dào); there is nothing more beautiful than virtue (dé). The Way and virtue are the great treasures of both the mundane and supramundane realms;
they are not sought through talent. Between having talent without virtue and having virtue without talent, it is better to have virtue without talent."
If even the worldly ways are thus, how much more so for those who aspire to the Buddhas and Patriarchs, seeking to transcend birth and death, refine the spirit, and return to quiescent extinction?
What is it that they study, such that you would question their ability? Now, I am but a blunt and unrefined man; I maintain my simplicity and rusticity, locking my door and having few concerns.
While this may suffice for the well-being of a single person, to preside over a monastic community, provide discipline for the monks, and shoulder the great responsibility of the Dharma-gate—
To erect the lofty banner of the Buddhas and Patriarchs requires more than mere talent or extraordinary ability; it demands long-standing refinement and proven competence.

How could one who lacks such preparation be capable of holding the office and bringing it to glory? Therefore, while managing a monastic community cannot do without talent, it must likewise avoid those who rely on their talent.
If those who rely on their talent advance, the harm they cause will not be slight. Thus, while one may promote talent, one must not fail to examine its character.

Virtue. The tradition of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not like the worldly method of employing men, which allows one to employ the greedy and the deceitful—those who are unconventional talents or unruly instruments that can be managed through the balance of expediency.
Yet, among these, the most difficult thing is that when Heaven fashions a person, those with complete talent are rare while those with partial talent abound;
those whose talent and virtue are combined are few, whereas those in whom they are not so combined are many.
He was numerous in his virtues. Observing him, he was sincere and grave; his speech followed the rules and his conduct adhered to the square.

He delighted in study and inquiry, and he delighted in cultivation and practice. His virtue was sufficient to command the respect of the multitude. Yet, when appointed to a task, his mind was hesitant and indecisive;

he was deficient on both the left and the right, unable to deploy even a single plan. What he lacked was talent, not virtue. When observing his talent, it was indeed nimble, dexterous, and quick-witted.
He dares to step forward; he is capable of elegance and capable of martial prowess. His talent is sufficient to respond to changing circumstances.

Yet, once entrusted with authority, he becomes envious of the worthy and jealous of the capable, stirring up the masses and creating disorder, while harboring his malice without revealing it. Those whom he suppresses...
This is virtue, not mere talent. Among those who serve as elders, who would not value virtue? Yet affairs cannot remain unmanaged.
Who would not pity talent? Yet those who ruin affairs cannot be allowed to remain.

There must be a way to refine and temper them—to mold, to strip away excess, and to polish them—so that both the firm and the supple may be put to use, and whether one is quick-witted or dull, all may be made effective.
"Discarded materials. This is also called "refining and exercising" so as to merely attend to affairs.

In attending to affairs, there are great and small, internal and external, left and right, and civil and martial. One who presides over a forest monastery cannot lack even one of these. Baizhang had insight into this;
thus, in establishing the Pure Rules (Qinggui), he first fixed the ten positions for the Head Officials (Toushou) and subsequently proceeded to the ranks [of the assembly].

The administration is like the court’s employment of officials: they are spread out like stars and arrayed like chess pieces, linked like silk threads and bound like ropes, ensuring that heads and eyes protect one another and fingers and arms defend one another.
When they are employed appropriately, the monastic community becomes orderly and disciplined, and the Way of the Dharma proceeds.

This is not done out of a deliberate intent to suppress or exalt, or to create high and low; rather, it is because individuals possess varying degrees of talent—some excellent and some mediocre—and their innate dispositions differ.
There are differences in the depth and breadth of their capacities; there are distinctions between superior and inferior abilities, and between broad and narrow magnitudes of character.

One must employ them according to these abilities so that each person’s talent is properly matched to the task. However, a monastic community (conglin) exists specifically to refine people's roots and transform their dispositions;

it should not allow things to remain in their natural state. Rather, one must provide many "forges" (training environments), selecting the most outstanding to inspire the multitude and purging those who are indolent.

This serves to discipline the remainder; when rewards and punishments are clear and distinct, the essential tasks will be accomplished. This is the great framework for governing the monastic community (seng-lin), and it must not be allowed to fall into disorder.

As for those who possess outstanding talent and character, whose fundamental understanding of the core principles is already clear, and who may be expected to become future leaders, they must be subjected to even more thorough training and refinement; they must not be permitted to proceed with ease. — From the *Dongxu* (Eastern Sequence).
From the lowest rank upward, the *yuezhong* (Joy-Maker) leads the assembly in solemn chanting; the *zhisui* (Year-Manager) oversees communal affairs;

the *dianzuo* (Director of the Kitchen) presides over cooking; the *zhiku* (Storekeeper) manages accounting; the *fusi* (Assistant Abbot) assists in general administration; the *weina* (Rector) maintains the regulations of the hall;

and the *jianyuan* (Superintendent) and *duisi* (Chief Administrator) take charge of the monastery’s business. Should these positions not be filled by those with sufficient experience, disorder will manifest before one, and the institution will inevitably fall into neglect and ruin.
Yet they were not so managed. In the western corridor, positions ranged from the lowly to the honored;

thus, the attendants (*śi-tse*) remained close to the elders, whether burning incense, attending to robes and bowls, or providing medicinal decoctions and recording correspondence—all for the sake of facilitating their studies. The *Chih-k'e* (Guest Manager) was responsible for receiving visitors;
the *Chih-yu* (Bath Manager) oversaw communal bathing practices; the *Chih-tsang* (Library Manager) presided over the precious scriptures; and the *Shu-chi* (Secretary) governed literary affairs.

The ink [marks] are applied. Regarding the head positions of the boards within the hall: the Hall Master (*tangzhu*) and the Rear Hall Master (*houtang*) occupy the first tier; ascending further, one finds the West Hall Master (*xitang*) and the Head Seat (*shouzuo*).

As for the duties of those who hold these four board-head positions, they are to regulate the Buddha-dharma to assist the Elder (*changlao*), and to forge the assembly of practitioners to welcome those who come to study;
thus, the affairs [of the monastery] are fully prepared. As the ancients said: "If one does not encounter gnarled roots and knotted branches, there is no way to test the strength of the axe."

One must employ distinct and sharp tools. Even if there are capable individuals, if they do not pass through the various administrative duties, how can their moral vessels be refined and their intellectual capacities be fully integrated?
It is not by relying on mere superficial practice that one succeeds; rather, it is when one is hampered by constraints that one lacks true talent.

How, then, could those who preside over a monastic community avoid failure and collapse? Furthermore, since ancient times, those of supreme acumen have sought to polish and sharpen human talent. This is the essential task of the monastic community.

There is no one who has not served as a *ling-li* (attendant). Gufo Muzhou was appointed by Baizhang to serve as the *dian-zuo* (steward); the great elder Xuefeng was entrusted by Deshan to serve as the *fan-tou* (head cook).

Furthermore, Yangqi himself served as the *bao-ku-si* (treasurer), while Yangshan and Xuedou served as the *zhi-ke* (guest master), Yunfeng as the *hua-zhu* (fund-raiser), Wuzu as the *mo-tou* (grindstone attendant), Miaoxi as the *dong-si* (latrine attendant), Bailin as the *zhi-yu* (bath attendant), and Yuancong as the *zhi-zhong* (general supervisor). Thus it returned.

The Stone Supervisor, the Acting Year-Manager, the Rectifier of the Bucket-Head, the Incense-Lamp Attendant of Dongshan, the Great Elder in charge of the Sui, and Lu Shen of the Lower Board—all these took the lead in ascetic practices.

This was done to nurture their capacities, to weather their talents, to shape their substance with axes and adzes, and to harden their sinews and bones with frost and snow, so that they might bear heavy burdens and travel far, serving as pillars for the Dharma-gate. Yet, this alone does not suffice for the transmission of the lineage.
First matter: Why is it that one must invariably be appointed as the Head Seat (shouzuo) or the West Hall (xitang), rather than simply being placed among the ranks of officials?
It is because we expect them to shoulder the burden of the Dharma; only by being able to forge and refine the monks can they truly benefit those yet to come.

Since we entrust them with the authority to govern the monastic community, they must be able to roar like a lion in the midst of the assembly; otherwise, they cannot succeed in perpetuating the life of wisdom. This applies if one is not among the board of leaders.

At that time, one must refine them with the hammer and tongs so that their fangs and claws become fierce and potent; one must promote those who hold the whisk so that their reputation and brilliance spread far and wide.
Once they occupy this position and issue these commands, how could they fail to "grasp the collar and expose the elbow"?

Alas, I observe that in the Dharma-gate of recent times, there is no discourse on forging and refining; instead, there is a haste to gather disciples. When a monk enters the gate, he is granted transmission in a perfunctory manner.
This refers to those administrative officials who, disregarding established precedents for seniority, treat their duties with casual negligence.

Wherever they go to various monasteries, they immediately say, "I have assigned such-and-such a person as the attendant," "I have assigned such-and-such as the guest prefect," "I have assigned such-and-such as the head of the quarters or the steward," and so on, even down to saying, "I have assigned such-and-such as a member of the meditation assembly.
Yet, in the end, they do not appoint them to actual positions of authority to test their mettle or put them to the test in difficult circumstances.
The head of the assembly sharpens their fangs and claws, forges their talents and abilities, and accumulates their reputation.

Yet, when faced with such matters, they turn their backs like a blind man facing a wall and immediately strike a single seal of approval. Knowing full well that one is weak and lacking, they merely bestow an empty title.
Not only do they mislead the common people of the world, but they also deceive themselves; their gateway is overturned and cannot be propped up. What is there to be gained from this?
Ah! One must also know that since antiquity there have been no Buddhas or patriarchs who made things easy, nor any elders who lacked capability.

An elder is one who serves as a model for devas and humans, presides over the dragon-elephants (the great disciples), acts as a standard for the heroic and the wise, and serves as the balance for both civil and military affairs.
Thus, they must possess the Way and its Virtue (*moral*) by which to instruct others, as well as the requisite talents to manage affairs.

Although their practice may be hidden and their application subtle—appearing as if ignorant or dull-witted—once entrusted with a great responsibility, they can weave the warp and woof and execute precise cuts with eyes that see no whole ox [before them].

Is this not because they have been thoroughly refined and tempered in the furnace and bellows of a master from an early age? Therefore, one must forge and refine those at the initial stage of their practice.
To hope for them to open their eyes, nothing is more effective than striking; to temper those who have long practiced, nothing is more refined than rigorous selection.

To expect the emergence of a host of eminent and worthy men without following this path, or to trample upon the ancestral temple, may well result in some fortunate exceptions, yet it is not the constant Dharma.
As the saying goes: "To lead the people to battle without having trained them is called abandoning them. This is truly a cause for lamentation.
This is precisely what causes one to weep with tears streaming down and heave long, deep sighs.

I have now carefully and solemnly completed the thirteenth discourse on the principles of transmission and refinement, setting them forth before you. Nevertheless, if one wishes to achieve a good beginning and a good end, the manner of its dissemination should be appropriate.
Be cautious. Why? If one possesses Buddha-nature, then all shall undergo tempering. Once tempered, the human spirit can be awakened.
While everyone is capable of awakening, it is not necessary that everyone be entrusted with the transmission.

An ancient once said that only those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence may practice Chan; I have often refuted this statement as being incorrect. This is because within the furnace and the bellows...

Just as a skilled physician uses molten, dull iron to treat a patient, if one does not apply the refinement of tempering, even those with superior faculties and sharp intelligence will become useless instruments;
how much more so those of lesser capacity? One who is skilled at tempering can turn even dull iron and a sickly patient into excellent material;
how much more so those of superior capacity? All who possess the aspiration for enlightenment can become Buddhas; all who possess the Buddha-nature can attain awakening.

The Way resides solely with the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). Through searching, selecting, scraping away impurities, and polishing the luster, when the defilements are exhausted, the clarity manifests—just as in the analogy of polishing a mirror.
Today, rather than faulting the lack of skillful means in their training, people generally claim that those of inferior capacity are utterly devoid of the opportunity for study and practice.

This is a delusion that has persisted for ten thousand ages, and it is something for which I gnash my teeth in indignation. Yet, it is said that once one undergoes awakening through investigation, [the Way is realized].
"You may entrust [the Dharma] to them all. This, however, is to know the first while remaining ignorant of the second.

One who has mastered the study of the house (the lineage) and is worthy of being entrusted with the Dharma must possess the eye of the Way capable of binding together the patriarchs, whose conduct and virtue can serve as a model for humans and devas, whose learning and knowledge can instruct those who come after, and whose skillful means can subdue fellow monks; only then should they be charged with the task of leaving the world."
To take this as being for the sake of human beings is like a seal being passed from one seal to another; the impression is perfectly replicated, and thus the Dharma-gate may truly be relied upon.

Even in the age of the Final Dharma (mappō), when it is difficult to find those who rely entirely [on the truth] and hard to seek out those with different capacities, one must necessarily dwell together for a long time and become intimately acquainted with their mental conduct.

Even if one cannot transcend the school or possess a unique perspective, one will at least not encounter a situation where a square base meets a round lid; there will surely be several who excel in this regard.
It is said: "One must first approximate the line and the square before one may serve as an elder or a presiding master of a retreat.
Furthermore, such a person must possess clear insight into the Way, enter correctly into the ranks of the Dharma, and have the sturdy backbone of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

They must maintain a strict integrity, refraining from entering fields of standing grain. This is by no means a position suitable for those who are mediocre, vulgar, foolish, inferior, treacherous, biased, or depraved."
This is an intrusion. Nevertheless, as for the Dharma-gate up to the present day, its degeneration and abuses are beyond description.

Whenever I see those who preside over the Dharma merely adhering to dead rules without subjecting themselves to the rigorous training of the body, it is truly difficult to find someone capable of awakening through such means.

Because those who have realized the source are difficult to find, and fearing that the lineage might be severed, one cannot help but urgently transmit it even to those who possess only a partial understanding.
There are two reasons for this: first, they value only the fundamental essence while disregarding the formal structures and principles;
lacking the skill to seize, shift, or transform another's mental state, they fall into a "one-stick Zen. Consequently, anyone who is merely clever with their tongue can obtain it.
They sneak past the barrier, yet they fail to undergo the rigorous training of the latter half of the path, ultimately leaving it unaddressed;

this is why the superficial gateways are so easy to transmit. Second, although the elder may wish to select worthy vessels, since no one can emerge from beneath the bamboo staff, he cannot bear the silence of solitude. He knows full well that these are outsiders and newcomers. One...
They possess only a half-understanding and do not accord with the numerical categories [of the path]. Yet their momentum makes it impossible to detain or hinder them;
if one attempts even a slight discernment, they will surely shake their heads and depart. This lack of refinement is why they end up being so numerous and widespread.
In my view, what is easily obtained should be scrutinized, yet you regard it as difficult to find as a tortoise’s hair or a rabbit’s horn; this is how you should respond to the difficulty.
To entrust [the Dharma] and yet regard it with such ease— as if merely conferring a dharma-name or admitting a disciple into the precepts— is this not a profound perversion?
If one truly desires that the orthodox lineage of Caoxi have deep roots and a long stream, and that the life-force of the successive patriarchs be authentically transmitted and correctly bestowed,
then regarding the act of appointing a dharma-heir, one ought to exhort and re-exhort, and command caution and further caution, so that together—
Fortify its walls and ramparts; heighten its embankments and defenses so that not even a shadow, a reflection, or a sound shall be heard beyond them.

If these are transmitted once and then again, and eventually lead to the breaking of the enclosure and the corruption of the orthodoxy, then the Dharma-gate will not fall into ruin. If this is so, one might ask:

"How is it that there were venerable seniors of former generations who strictly guarded the keys and, until their deaths, did not transmit them to a single person? The answer is: This was surely because they knew well [the circumstances].
When consciousness is moved by indignation, it may act with excessive rectitude; this occurs only when there is no other choice, yet even so, it is not the Middle Way.

The life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs has been transmitted from generation to generation, and the passing down of the robe and Dharma serves as the seed of illumination for ten thousand generations.
While it is certainly not right to bestow these teachings indiscriminately, how could it ever be considered correct to ultimately sever them? Have you not seen the world...?
The Venerable One and the patriarchs of the Western Heaven, whenever transmitting the Dharma, would invariably speak with earnest concern, saying:
"Transmit it to those who shall come; do not allow it to be severed. Yet, in the interim, there were sometimes people and sometimes none; sometimes there was much bestowed and sometimes little.
Each has its own fixed allotment, which cannot be forced or contrived; it is simply a matter of attaining what is appropriate. Mazu produced eighty good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitras).
There were four men, each serving as a patriarch; none were unworthy of their capacities.
Among those who later became renowned for the extreme abundance of their talent were Yunmen, Dongshan, Fayan, Fenyang, Huanglong Nan, Zhenjing Wen, Dongsan, Yuanwu, and Miaoxi.
As for the lineage transmitted by Miaoxi, the genealogical records list over ninety individuals.
Never has anyone questioned the elders for making excessive transmissions.

As for those who transmitted the robe and bowl through a single line—such as Fengxue, Yangqi, Baiyun, Ying’an, Mian, and others—though they received the lineage alone and were capable of upholding the family tradition, they likewise never considered severing the line to be the mark of excellence.
If one must consider severing the line to be the mark of excellence, then...
Why did the Fourth Patriarch need to travel so far from Mount Lu to Niutou? Why did Nanyue need to grind bricks?
Why did the Boatman need to capsize his boat? Why did Fengxue need to wail in grief? And why did Dayang need to offer his topknot and hide shoes?
To entrust one’s *zhiduo* (formal robe) to Fushan was to seek a true vessel of the Dharma.

Whether acting as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), whether initiating new developments or maintaining established traditions, whether providing restorative aid or responding to the exigencies of the times, each has their own profound dedication; they must not be lightly criticized.

At such a time, the era was flourishing; Buddhas and patriarchs appeared, and dragons and elephants gathered. There were those whose wisdom surpassed that of their teachers, and others who at least emulated them.
Among those who are equal to the Master, there is not one within the vast precincts who is not a vessel for the Dharma.
Even if one entrusts the teaching to several dozen, or even a hundred people, it is not considered too many. The Dharma ought to be propagated; it must be propagated. This is the current age.
The masters lack the discernment to verify students, while the learners pursue empty fame. Thus, though several may be entrusted with the lineage, there is not a single one who is truly qualified.
Regarding those worthy of being entrusted [with the Dharma], there were perhaps several dozen people, yet not a single one was truly a mature elder who had transcended the world.
They were like sheep wearing tiger skins, deceiving and seducing one another; thus, even if one person were entrusted, it would already be incorrect.

Consequently, true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) would rather let the lineage be severed than allow them to run off in pursuit of solitary loftiness as a means of "remedy. For the Dharma must be remedied, and it cannot be otherwise.
It is not a matter of remediation. For knowledge that functions through expansion is easy, while knowledge that functions through remediation is difficult.

The easy has its own merits; the difficult likewise has its own benefits. Although it is said that the knowledge of remediation is not transmitted, it stands as a central pillar amidst the turbulent current;
the eye of the Way remains fully present, its radiance shining brightly throughout a hundred generations.
Can this be called severance? Though it may overflow the gateway and courtyard, and though much may be entrusted, if one waters melons at midday, where will the fruit be?
If, before even a blink of an eye, things fall into ruin and disorder, can this be called continuity?

In short, if you clarify the fundamental principles and understand the tempering process, then the first step will not be difficult to emerge from. After awakening, do not lightly let go; be cautious and diligent.

Its transmission and circulation are both blessings for the Dharma-gate. To destroy its fundamental principles and neglect its refinement would result in the fault of allowing the stream of transmission to become turbid;
yet to be overly cautious would carry the anxiety of severing it entirely—neither is a blessing for the Dharma-gate.
Nevertheless, a true spiritual friend acts as a Buddha or Patriarch entering the grass to seek out people, opening the eyes of humans and devas; how could they possibly...

Be cautious not to be indiscriminate; it is better to have few that are authentic than many that are false. Do not allow weeds, wild grasses, *liang*, *you*, *ti*, and *bai* to confuse the noble seeds.
Only then will the life of wisdom (*hui-ming*) surely endure forever and flourish greatly.

Therefore, I have spoken with bitter earnestness and exerted effort in this discourse on refinement, concluding with an exhortation to be careful in its transmission as the final word. For the fundamental principles and the ancestral lineage are of the utmost importance. Diligence...
"Tempering," "maintaining vigilance," and "this third dharma"—all of these are things unheard of in the world and difficult to practice.
To repeat them again and again is certain to offend taboos; yet, if one wishes to cause the True Eye to circulate and descendants to gain strength, the Way must necessarily pass through this.
As the saying goes: "When speaking, do not avoid cutting out one's tongue. Confucius said: "Only the Spring and Autumn Annals can truly understand me."
"Alas! Those who will find fault with me will likely be those of the *Chunqiu*. For now, I shall preserve this theory to await the arrival of future sages.
If, after a thousand or ten thousand generations, another like Ziyun should appear, he will surely recognize Ziyun."
Postscript on the Discourse on Forging in the Chan Gate:

I have indeed observed that in recent times, the Chan gate has clung tenaciously to established conventions and lacks proficiency in forging and refining. Consequently, the True Doctrine has often become desolate and the flow of the Dharma has been severed.
Having no other recourse, I have established these new methods as a last resort, like attempting to treat a dead horse with medicine. As for the discussion...
A single stroke of the fundamental portion—attaining realization before words is still being stuck in the shell and lost in the seal.
Mastering the meaning beneath the phrase is already a wild view encountered at every turn. Awakening is indeed not absent, yet how can one avoid falling into the "second head"?

To be so frantic about discussing tongs and hammers, debating forging and tempering—is this not placing a head upon a head, or speaking a dream within a dream? You who play with lumps of mud, come forward!
To regard things as substantial dharmas and fail to understand their shifting transformations brings misfortune upon this mountain monk, who is thus cast alive into the Iron Ring Mountains.

As for Tan-yuan’s "perfect circle," were it to encounter Yangshan’s single spark, it would be consumed by fire. At that time, this mountain monk would join his palms and say, "A true master! A true master! This would be one who truly knows how to employ Sun Tzu’s art of war, rather than being like Zhao Kuo discussing military strategy.
